extraction.name: Natural Questions
extraction.description: Natural Questions (NQ) is a question answering dataset consisting of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine, paired with Wikipedia pages from the top 5 search results. Annotators identify long answers (typically a paragraph or table) and short answers (one or more entities) if present on the page, or mark null if no answer is present. The public release contains 307,373 training examples with single annotations, 7,830 development examples with 5-way annotations, and 7,842 test examples with 5-way annotations.

extraction.rai:dataCollection: Questions were sampled from real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine (queries of 8 words or more issued by multiple users in a short period of time), filtered using heuristics to retain fact-seeking questions. Each filtered question was run through the Google search engine and paired with a Wikipedia page from the top 5 search results. The resulting (question, Wikipedia page) pairs were presented to a pool of around 50 human annotators who identified long and short answers.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web API; Manual Human Curator; User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries from the Google search engine query stream; Wikipedia pages returned in the top 5 search results for each query.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were presented with a (question, Wikipedia page) pair and asked to complete three stages: (1) Question Identification — determine if the question is good or bad; (2) Long Answer Identification — select the earliest HTML bounding box (paragraph, table, list item, or whole list) containing enough information to answer the question, or mark 'no answer'; (3) Short Answer Identification — select the entity or set of entities within the long answer, flag yes/no, or mark no short answer possible. A pool of around 50 annotators performed annotations with an average annotation time of 80 seconds. Comprehensive guidelines were developed and annotation quality was constantly monitored. Post-hoc quality evaluation used four expert annotators (guideline authors) who independently judged correctness and then reached consensus judgments categorizing answers as Correct (C), Correct but debatable (Cd), or Wrong (W).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Post-hoc precision was estimated by sampling 139 examples, having four experts independently classify each as C, Cd, or W, then reaching consensus judgments; precision was defined as the proportion of C and Cd items. For variability analysis, 25-way annotations were collected on 302 examples and the proportion of non-null annotations per item (μ) was correlated with expert consensus judgments. For development and test evaluation, 5-way annotations were used with a threshold of β=2 (at least 2 of 5 annotators must give a non-null answer for the system to be required to answer). A 'super-annotator' upper bound was constructed from 20-way annotations to approximate the posterior distribution over answers.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 for training examples; 5 for development and test examples; 25 for a subset of 302 examples used for variability analysis
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Google's Cloud NLP API (used for part-of-speech tagging and entity identification during question filtering); Hearst patterns (used to identify categorical noun phrases for question filtering)
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Questions are drawn from Google search engine queries, which may introduce biases; Wikipedia is used as the evidence source, which like any dataset may have biases in this choice
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Questions are limited to those 8 words or more in length; 'how to' questions are excluded; evidence documents are restricted to Wikipedia pages; future data collection efforts may introduce shorter queries, 'how to' questions, or domains other than Wikipedia
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Large-scale end-to-end training data for the question answering problem; benchmark for evaluating question answering systems; driving research in natural language understanding
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions were filtered from the Google search query stream using heuristics to retain fact-seeking questions of 8 words or more (e.g., starting with 'who', 'when', or 'where' followed by specific grammatical patterns, or containing multiple entities with certain part-of-speech features). Queries were then run through the Google search engine and only kept if a Wikipedia page appeared in the top 5 search results. Part-of-speech tags and entities were identified using Google's Cloud NLP API.
